newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexican editor pays bail after arrest on tax charge.
newsitem.headline: Mexican editor pays bail after arrest on tax charge.

text.p: One of Mexico's leading newspapers accused the government of censorship on Friday after police ordered the arrest of its editor on charges of tax fraud.

Juan Francisco Ealy Ortiz, editor of El Universal newspaper, surrendered to authorities on Friday morning vowing to fight allegations he had defrauded tax authorities of $5.4 million over the past two years.
He was released on Friday night after paying a $1.5 million bond.

"I am innocent," Ealy told dozens of reporters upon his release and before entering his armour-plated Mercedes-Benz. "El Universal will continue forward. It must keep fighting for the rule of law, especially freedom of the press."
Dozens of heavily armed police raided El Universal's offices on Thursday night in a fruitless attempt to find Ealy. Agents pointed automatic weapons at his personal assistant but left empty-handed.
The action drew protests from the newspaper, which described it as a crude attempt to silence it after it shifted from reliable government ally to a new, more critical stance.

Roberto Rock, El Universal's editorial director, said on Friday the newspaper was suffering "political repression by the government" and accused hardline Interior Minister Emilio Chauyffet of ordering the arrest. "We have received warnings about the government's irritation and dissatisfaction with the newspaper's editorial line," he told Radio Red.
Reforma, a competing newspaper, said government press chiefs had decided this month to cut off all official advertising in El Universal out of annoyance at its new anti-government line.

El Universal itself said in a full-page advertisement on Friday: "The unjustified and violent (police) operation as well as a growing wave of pressure and aggression orchestrated against the newspaper are the result of a government decision to silence the critical and committed editorial line taken on by this editorial organisation."
Tomas Ruiz, Finance Ministry tax chief, denied any attack on press freedom. "What we are talking about is the strict application of the law. No one is exempt from that," he said.

In a country with a tradition of government meddling in the press, El Universal raised eyebrows this year when it started hiring well-known anti-government columnists and running big front-page stories attacking official corruption.
Previously the paper toed the government line and followed the widely accepted practice in Mexican media of allowing reporters to accept favours from officials in return for favourable coverage.

Reporters said Ealy apparently decided to take President Ernesto Zedillo's promises to open up Mexico's closed political system and promote greater democracy at face value. But some competitors also recalled that Ealy, who had profited for years under the old system of government patronage, made an unlikely defender of press ethics.
Reforma said presidential aides were irritated at what they saw as a double standard at El Universal: "They attack (the government) with their pens but they accept all kinds of favours."
Friday's case was not the first time in recent weeks that the government appeared to have applied tax laws strictly against political opponents.

INDEMERC-Louis Harris, a local polling organisation, complained last month that tax authorities had swooped on it shortly after it published a poll showing the ruling Institutional Revolutionary Party in last place among voters in the Mexican capital.
